milestones.title: Naniwa becomes the imperial capital
milestones.detail: Emperor Kōtoku moves the court to Naniwa on the Uemachi Plateau, beside the port of Naniwa-tsu. The Naniwa Nagara-Toyosaki Palace is completed in 652 and the court returns to Asuka in 655.

milestones.title: Naniwa is briefly capital again
milestones.detail: Emperor Shōmu declares the rebuilt Naniwa Palace the capital; the court moves back to Nara the following year. Naniwa remains the main port linking the Yamato court with Korea and China.

milestones.title: Ishiyama Hongan-ji founded
milestones.detail: Jōdo Shinshū Buddhists establish a fortified temple headquarters on the site of the old palace, and a temple town grows around it. Oda Nobunaga besieges it from 1570 and the temple is razed on its surrender.

milestones.title: Toyotomi Hideyoshi begins Osaka Castle
milestones.detail: Hideyoshi starts building his castle on the temple site; the main keep is finished in 1585 and the whole castle in 1597. A castle town grows around it.

milestones.title: Siege of Osaka: castle and town destroyed
milestones.detail: Tokugawa forces take Osaka Castle in the summer campaign of 1615, ending the Toyotomi line. The keep burns and the town is devastated, but recovers quickly.

milestones.title: Shogunate rebuilds the castle and city
milestones.detail: Having taken Osaka under direct rule in 1619, the Tokugawa shogunate rebuilds the castle from 1620 on a larger scale, with a new keep finished in 1626. Canals and warehouse districts make Osaka the country's commercial centre.

milestones.title: Dōjima Rice Exchange established
milestones.detail: Rice merchants gather at Dōjima, where the rice exchange is set up in 1697. It later develops what is regarded as the world's first futures market.

milestones.title: Ōshio Heihachirō's uprising burns a quarter of the city
milestones.detail: A low-ranking samurai leads an uprising over the city's failure to help its poor. About one quarter of Osaka is burned before the rising is put down.

milestones.title: Osaka opened to foreign trade
milestones.detail: Osaka is opened to foreign trade on 1 January 1868, and a foreign settlement is laid out at Kawaguchi. The castle falls to imperial forces the same year.

milestones.title: City of Osaka incorporated
milestones.detail: The four urban wards become Osaka City, covering 15.27 square kilometres. The city becomes an industrial centre led by textiles.

milestones.title: First boundary extension
milestones.detail: Osaka annexes towns and villages of Nishinari and Higashinari districts, growing from 15 to 55.67 square kilometres.

milestones.title: 'Great Osaka': Japan's largest city
milestones.detail: The second boundary extension absorbs the rest of the two neighbouring districts. At the 1925 census Osaka has 2,114,804 people, more than Tokyo City.

milestones.title: Municipal subway opens
milestones.detail: The first section of the Osaka municipal subway opens between Umeda and Shinsaibashi, the first publicly run subway in Japan.

milestones.title: Air raids destroy central Osaka
milestones.detail: The first great raid, on the night of 13-14 March 1945, burns out 21 square kilometres of the city. More than 10,000 civilians die in the raids of March to August.

milestones.title: Expo '70
milestones.detail: The first world's fair held in Asia runs from 15 March to 13 September 1970 at Suita, in Osaka's northern suburbs.

milestones.title: Expo 2025 on Yumeshima
milestones.detail: Osaka hosts a second World Expo from April to October 2025 on the reclaimed island of Yumeshima in Osaka Bay.

notes: Start date is contested. 645 is used because the move of the capital to Naniwa is recorded in the Nihon Shoki and the palace has been excavated on the Uemachi Plateau, at the centre of today's city. Earlier claims exist: Shitennō-ji is traditionally dated to 593 (also from the Nihon Shoki; it would be a defensible alternative start), the port of Naniwa-tsu was active in the 5th century, a palace at Osumi is mentioned for 390-430, and Sumiyoshi Taisha has a legendary founding of 211. A later convention dates the present city from 1496 (Ishiyama Hongan-ji) or 1583 (Osaka Castle); the name Osaka dates only from that period. Settlement on the site between the 8th and 15th centuries was a port and temple town, not a large city. Population: no figure of any kind was found for 645-1579, so the series starts with Chandler's 1580 estimate and the app should show no estimate for the first 930 years. Figures for 1665-1862 are the registered townspeople of the three Osaka districts (Sangō), a real count that leaves out the small samurai population and the suburbs beyond the three districts; Chandler's estimates of the total for the same period are similar (for example 380,000 in 1700, 383,000 in 1800). Figures for 1873-1945 are for the city as bounded at each date, so the jumps at 1897 and 1925 are boundary extensions; register-based counts before 1920 overstate the population and police-survey counts were preferred where available. The UN series from 1950 covers the whole Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto built-up agglomeration, several times the municipal figure, so expect a large step at 1950. Landmarks: heights of the two lost castle keeps are reconstructions from plans, marked estimated. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Shitennō-ji (founded 593, present buildings 1963), Sumiyoshi Taisha, Osaka City Central Public Hall and Kyocera Dome. The Tower of the Sun stands in Suita, about 13 km north of the city centre, inside the urban area.
